title: SCBench: A KV Cache-Centric Analysis of Long-Context Methods
one_line_claim: KV cache compression methods suffer catastrophic multi-turn degradation in shared-context scenarios despite initial single-query performance.
method_summary: SCBench benchmarks eight long-context solution categories (linear RNNs, sparse attention, KV cache dropping, quantization, retrieval, prompt compression) across 12 tasks on 8 LLMs, tracking performance through four KV cache lifecycle stages: generation, compression, retrieval, and loading.

key_findings.finding: At 1/32 compression ratio, StreamingLLM achieves only 15.5% average performance versus 48.7% baseline on Llama-3.1-8B.
key_findings.quote: At 1/32 compression (3% retention), methods like StreamingLLM achieve only 15.5% average performance on Llama-3.1-8B versus 48.7% baseline.

key_findings.finding: Sub-O(n) memory methods maintain accuracy on first queries but lose accuracy in subsequent requests, failing in multi-turn scenarios.
key_findings.quote: sub-O(n) memory methods perform well on the first query but lose accuracy in subsequent requests in multi-turn scenarios

key_findings.finding: Exact-match retrieval tasks with incompressible content trigger sharp performance cliffs at 1/4 compression ratios.
key_findings.quote: sub-O(n) memory methods experience a sharp performance drop at a 1/4 compression rate, particularly on exact-match retrieval tasks

relation_to_herald.shared: Both focus on KV cache compression as the primary hazard vector; both target multi-turn generation scenarios where accumulated KV state drives failures; both evaluate compression across multiple LLM scales and ratios.
differs_on: HERALD predicts failures pre-onset from per-token logit features using XGBoost; SCBench benchmarks realized failures post-hoc via accuracy metrics on fixed tasks.
HERALD treats the compressor as a black box and operates during generation; SCBench evaluates specific compressor algorithms at design time.
HERALD targets catastrophic non-termination and looping; SCBench measures task-level accuracy degradation on semantic and retrieval tasks.
